blocks.text: A furnace wall, a brake disc and a heat sink all have one thing in common: temperature varies through them and decides whether they survive. Finite element thermal analysis turns the heat conduction equation into the same kind of matrix problem as a stress analysis, with temperatures at nodes in place of displacements and heat flows in place of forces.

blocks.markdown: **Governing equation and weak form.** For steady one-dimensional conduction in a rod of area $A$ (m$^2$) and conductivity $k$ (W/(m K)), energy balance gives $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(kA\dfrac{dT}{dx}\right)+Q=0$ with temperature $T$ (K or degrees Celsius, only differences matter) and internal heat generation $Q$ (W/m). This has exactly the structure of the bar equation $(EA\,u')'+b=0$, so the same weak form and linear shape functions apply: $T$ replaces $u$, $kA$ replaces $EA$ and heat flow replaces force.

blocks.caption: Two-node conduction element (W/K) and the assembled system; F has units W

blocks.title: Thermal boundary conditions
blocks.text: A **prescribed temperature** is an essential condition (it removes a degree of freedom). A **prescribed heat flux** $q$ (W/m$^2$) adds the load $qA$ (W) to the node. **Convection** to an ambient at $T_\infty$ with film coefficient $h$ (W/(m$^2$ K)) is a natural condition $-k\,dT/dx=h(T-T_\infty)$: it adds $hA$ to the diagonal of $\mathbf K$ at that node and $hAT_\infty$ to the load vector. An **insulated** surface has zero flux and needs no entry.

blocks.markdown: **Assembly for two elements.** Number the nodes 1, 2, 3 along the rod. Each element contributes its $2\times2$ matrix to the rows and columns of its two nodes, so the shared node 2 receives the sum of both stiffnesses. With conductances $c_1=k_1A/L_1$ and $c_2=k_2A/L_2$ (W/K), the matrix has first row $c_1,\,-c_1,\,0$, second row $-c_1,\,c_1+c_2,\,-c_2$ and third row $0,\,-c_2,\,c_2$.

blocks.caption: Assembled conduction matrix of two elements in series

blocks.title: Furnace wall with convection
blocks.prompt: A composite wall of area $A=0.5$ m$^2$ has a steel layer ($k_1=45$ W/(m K), $L_1=20$ mm) and a refractory layer ($k_2=0.8$ W/(m K), $L_2=50$ mm). The inner face (node 1) is held at 500 degrees Celsius. The outer face (node 3) loses heat by convection with $h=25$ W/(m$^2$ K) to air at 30 degrees Celsius. Find the temperatures at nodes 2 and 3 using two elements.

steps.text: Conductances: $c_1=45(0.5)/0.02=1125$ W/K and $c_2=0.8(0.5)/0.05=8$ W/K. Convection at node 3 adds $hA=25(0.5)=12.5$ W/K to $K_{33}$ and $hAT_\infty=375$ W to $F_3$.
Node 1 has a prescribed temperature, so its row is eliminated and its coupling moves to the load: $F_2=c_1T_1=562500$ W.
The reduced system for $(T_2,T_3)$ has first row $c_1+c_2,\,-c_2$ (that is 1133, -8) and second row $-c_2,\,c_2+hA$ (that is -8, 20.5), with right-hand side $(562500,\,375)$ W.
Solving gives $T_2=497.97$ degrees Celsius and $T_3=212.62$ degrees Celsius.
Check with thermal resistances: $R=L_1/(k_1A)+L_2/(k_2A)+1/(hA)=0.2059$ K/W, so the heat flow is $q=470/R=2282.78$ W, and $T_3=30+q/(hA)=212.62$, in agreement.

blocks.answer: T2 = 497.97 and T3 = 212.62 degrees Celsius; heat flow 2282.78 W.

rows: Remove the row and column (or penalty)
Move known $T$ terms to the right
blocks.caption: How thermal boundary conditions enter the matrices

blocks.markdown: **Transient analysis.** With heat capacity the equation becomes $\mathbf C\,\dot{\mathbf T}+\mathbf K\mathbf T=\mathbf F$. The matrix $\mathbf C$ has entries $\rho cAL/2$ per node in lumped form, where $\rho$ is density (kg/m$^3$) and $c$ specific heat (J/(kg K)). The thermal diffusivity $\alpha=k/(\rho c)$ (m$^2$/s) measures how fast heat spreads. Explicit (forward Euler) integration with a lumped $\mathbf C$ is stable only if the Fourier number $\alpha\Delta t/h_e^2\le1/2$, so the step limit shrinks with the **square** of the element size $h_e$ (m). Implicit schemes (backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson) are unconditionally stable, but the step must still be small enough to resolve the temperature change in time.

blocks.caption: Explicit stability limit for linear 1D elements

blocks.title: Time step for an aluminium heat sink
blocks.prompt: A transient model of an aluminium heat sink uses linear elements of size $h_e=2$ mm. Typical properties: $k=200$ W/(m K), $\rho=2700$ kg/m$^3$, $c=900$ J/(kg K). Find the largest stable explicit time step for lumped and consistent capacity.

steps.text: Consistent capacity: $\Delta t\le h_e^2/(6\alpha)=0.0081$ s, a factor of 3 smaller.
Halving $h_e$ to 1 mm cuts both limits by 4, so the step limit becomes impractical for fine meshes; an implicit scheme is then preferred, with $\Delta t$ chosen to follow the heating transient.

blocks.answer: About 0.0243 s for lumped and 0.0081 s for consistent capacity.

rows: Cheap per step, tiny steps for fine meshes
May oscillate for very large steps

items: Assemble conduction matrices element by element; shared nodes add.
Apply prescribed temperatures by elimination; add flux and convection terms to $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf K$.
Solve $\mathbf K\mathbf T=\mathbf F$ and check the result with a thermal-resistance network.
For transient runs, compute $\alpha$ and the smallest element size and compare $\Delta t$ with $h_e^2/(2\alpha)$ before using an explicit scheme.

blocks.title: Convection changes the matrix
blocks.text: Convection is not a load only: it adds $hA$ to the stiffness diagonal. Omitting the diagonal term gives a wrong temperature, and also removes the only restraint of a model with no fixed temperature, making $\mathbf K$ singular.

points: The conduction element matrix is $\dfrac{kA}{L}[1,-1;-1,1]$ (W/K) and assembly adds shared-node terms.
Convection adds $hA$ to $K$ at the surface node and $hAT_\infty$ to $F$; prescribed flux adds $qA$; insulation adds nothing; prescribed temperature is essential.
Thermal diffusivity $\alpha=k/(\rho c)$ controls the speed of heat flow; explicit stability needs $\Delta t\le h_e^2/(2\alpha)$ for a lumped capacity matrix.
Step limits scale with element size squared, so refining the mesh by 2 shrinks the explicit step by 4.

questions.stem: Which matrix is the element conduction matrix of a two-node one-dimensional element of length $L$, area $A$ and conductivity $k$?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: conductance $kA/L$ relates heat flow to the temperature difference between the nodes, with the usual spring-like sign pattern.
distractorRationale.b: This is the thermal resistance, the reciprocal of the conductance.
distractorRationale.c: Positive off-diagonal terms would give heat flow proportional to the sum of the temperatures, not their difference.
distractorRationale.d: This resembles a capacity (mass) matrix, not a conduction matrix.

questions.explanation: A uniform temperature must produce zero net heat flow, so each row must sum to zero, giving the pattern $[1,-1;-1,1]$. The scale factor is the conductance $kA/L$ in W/K.

questions.stem: A rod end surface of area $A=2.5\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$ loses heat by convection with film coefficient $h=40$ W/(m$^2$ K) to air at $T_\infty=300$ K. In the FE model, find the load vector contribution $hAT_\infty$ at that node, in W.
questions.explanation: Convection adds $hA$ to the stiffness diagonal and $hAT_\infty$ to the load vector. Here $hA=40\times2.5\times10^{-3}=0.1$ W/K and $hAT_\infty=0.1\times300=30$ W.

questions.stem: What is the correct treatment of an insulated (adiabatic) end of a one-dimensional thermal model?

options.text: No term is added: zero flux is the natural boundary condition
Set the end temperature equal to the ambient temperature
Add $hA$ to the diagonal with a very large $h$
Add the flux $kA\,dT/dx$ as an unknown to the load vector

questions.correctOptionText: No term is added: zero flux is the natural boundary condition

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the natural condition $-k\,dT/dx=0$ is satisfied automatically in the weak form when no boundary term is added.
distractorRationale.b: Fixing the end temperature would be an essential condition and would force heat flow.
distractorRationale.c: A very large $h$ would tie the end to the ambient temperature, the opposite of insulation.
distractorRationale.d: The flux is zero, so there is nothing to add.

questions.explanation: In the weak form the boundary term is $w\,kA\,dT/dx$ at the end. For an adiabatic surface this flux is zero, so the term vanishes and no modification of the equations is needed.

questions.stem: Which of these thermal boundary conditions is an essential (Dirichlet) condition?

options.text: A surface held at a prescribed temperature by a coolant bath
A uniform heat flux applied by a heater

questions.correctOptionText: A surface held at a prescribed temperature by a coolant bath

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it prescribes the primary variable, temperature, and so removes a degree of freedom.
distractorRationale.b: Heat flux is a natural condition entered in the load vector.
distractorRationale.c: Convection is a natural (Robin) condition entering both the stiffness and load.
distractorRationale.d: Insulation is a natural condition with zero flux.

questions.explanation: Essential conditions are on the primary unknown $T$ and are imposed on the solution space. Flux and convection conditions involve $k\,dT/dx$ and enter the weak form's boundary term.

questions.stem: A steel rod of cross-section $A=1.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$ and conductivity $k=40$ W/(m K) is modelled with two equal elements of length 0.1 m each (nodes 1, 2, 3). Node 1 is held at 100 degrees Celsius, and node 3 loses heat by convection with $h=20$ W/(m$^2$ K) to air at 20 degrees Celsius acting on the end area $A$. Find the temperature at node 3 in degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The conductance per element is $kA/L=40(10^{-3})/0.1=0.4$ W/K and $hA=0.02$ W/K. Eliminating node 1, the equations are $0.8T_2-0.4T_3=0.4(100)$ and $-0.4T_2+0.42T_3=0.02(20)$. Solving gives $T_2=96.36$ and $T_3=92.73$ degrees Celsius. A resistance check gives $R=5+50=55$ K/W, $q=80/55=1.4545$ W and $T_3=20+50q=92.73$.

questions.stem: A steel component is meshed with linear elements of size $h_e=1.5$ mm. Typical properties: $k=45$ W/(m K), $\rho=7800$ kg/m$^3$, $c=470$ J/(kg K). Using a lumped capacity matrix and forward Euler integration, find the largest stable time step $\Delta t=h_e^2/(2\alpha)$ in seconds.
questions.explanation: The diffusivity is $\alpha=45/(7800\times470)=1.2275\times10^{-5}$ m$^2$/s. Then $\Delta t_{crit}=(1.5\times10^{-3})^2/(2\times1.2275\times10^{-5})=0.0916$ s. Beyond this step the explicit scheme becomes unstable.

questions.stem: An explicit transient thermal analysis is stable at a given time step. The mesh is then refined so that every element is half as large. By what factor must the stable time step be changed, all else being equal?

options.text: Reduced by a factor of 4, because the limit scales with the element size squared
Unchanged, because only the material sets the limit

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced by a factor of 4, because the limit scales with the element size squared

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the limit is $h_e^2/(2\alpha)$, so halving $h_e$ divides it by 4.
distractorRationale.b: A factor of 2 would apply to a wave problem where the limit scales with $h_e$, not to diffusion.
distractorRationale.c: The limit depends on both diffusivity and element size.
distractorRationale.d: A finer mesh makes the explicit limit stricter, not looser.

questions.explanation: For diffusion the stability limit scales as $h_e^2/\alpha$. This is why fine meshes make explicit thermal integration prohibitively slow and implicit schemes are used.

questions.stem: An implicit backward-Euler scheme is unconditionally stable for linear transient conduction, but a time step that is too large will still give a poorly resolved temperature history.
questions.explanation: True. Stability only means the solution does not blow up; the accuracy of a first-order scheme still depends on the step compared with the time scale of the temperature change. A step much larger than that time scale smears the transient.

questions.stem: A three-node rod has conductivity data $k_1=50$ W/(m K), $L_1=0.05$ m for element 1 and $k_2=10$ W/(m K), $L_2=0.025$ m for element 2, both with $A=4.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$. Assemble the global conduction matrix, and describe how you would apply a prescribed temperature at node 1, a heat flux of $q=500$ W/m$^2$ into node 3 and convection ($h=15$ W/(m$^2$ K), $T_\infty=25$ degrees Celsius) at node 3.
markingGuide: Node 1: essential condition, eliminate row and column and move $c_1T_1$ to the load of node 2
Convection: add $hA=15(0.004)=0.06$ W/K to $K_{33}$ and $hAT_\infty=1.5$ W to $F_3$
questions.explanation: Assembly sums contributions at shared nodes, while flux and convection are natural conditions that modify the load and diagonal. Only the prescribed temperature removes an equation.

questions.stem: Explain how the explicit time step for a transient thermal model is chosen from the element size and thermal diffusivity, and why implicit methods are used for fine meshes. State what limits the step in the implicit case.
markingGuide: Diffusivity $\alpha=k/(\rho c)$; explicit lumped stability $\Delta t\le h_e^2/(2\alpha)$ with the smallest $h_e$
Consistent capacity gives a stricter limit $h_e^2/(6\alpha)$
Limit scales with $h_e^2$, so halving the element size divides the step by 4
Implicit schemes (backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson) are unconditionally stable so fine meshes can use larger steps
In the implicit case the step is limited by accuracy: it must resolve the time scale of the temperature change and any time-varying load
questions.explanation: Explicit stability is a property of the smallest element and the diffusivity. Implicit methods remove that limit, leaving accuracy as the controlling factor.
